DRACULA: Hunting for the Actions Users Want Deep
Research Agents to Execute

Nishant Balepur Affiliation: University of Maryland   Affiliation: New York University   Email: nbalepur@umd.edu    Malachi Hamada Affiliation: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (Ai2) Email: aakankshan@allenai.org    Varsha Kishore Affiliation: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (Ai2)    Sergey Feldman Affiliation: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (Ai2)    Amanpreet Singh Affiliation: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (Ai2)    Pao Siangliulue Affiliation: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (Ai2)    Joseph Chee Chang Affiliation: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (Ai2)    Rachel Rudinger Affiliation: University of Maryland      Eunsol Choi Affiliation: New York University      Jordan Boyd-Graber Affiliation: University of Maryland      Doug Downey Affiliation: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (Ai2)    Aakanksha Naik Affiliation: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (Ai2)
Abstract

Scientific Deep Research (DR) agents answer user queries by synthesizing research papers into multi-section reports. User feedback can improve their utility, but existing protocols only score the final report, making it hard to study and learn which intermediate actions DR agents should take to improve reports. We collect DRACULA, the first dataset with user feedback on intermediate actions for DR. Over five weeks, nineteen expert CS researchers ask queries to a DR system that proposes actions (e.g., “Add a section on datasets’’). Our users select actions they prefer, then judge whether an output report applied their selections successfully, yielding 8,103 action preferences and 5,230 execution judgments. After confirming a DR agent can execute DRACULA’s actions, we study the predictability of user-preferred actions via simulation---how well LLMs predict the actions users select---a step toward learning to generate useful actions. We discover: (1) LLM judges initially struggle to predict action selections, but improve most when using a user’s full selection history, rather than self-reported or extrapolated user context signals; (2) Users’ selections for the same query differ based on unstated goals, bottlenecking simulation and motivating affordances that let users steer reports; and (3) Our simulation results inform an online intervention that generates new actions based on the user’s past interactions, which users pick most often in follow-up studies. Overall, while work extensively studies execution, DRACULA reveals a key challenge is deciding which actions to execute in the first place. We open-source DRACULA’s study design, user feedback, and simulation tasks to spur work on action feedback for long-horizon agents.11 1 Our data and code are available at: https://github.com/allenai/dracula.

11footnotetext: Work primarily completed during internship at Ai2.

1 Introduction: User Feedback in Deep Research Could Use More Bite

Scientific Deep Research (DR) agents synthesize scientific papers into long-form reports in response to user queries (Asai et al., 2024). Even when DR agents excel on offline benchmarks (Wei et al., 2025), user feedback remains key to improving their utility (Ouyang et al., 2022).

Most work collects user feedback on the final DR report with pairwise (Zhao et al., 2025a) or absolute ratings (Hwang et al., 2026). However, such approaches do not let users directly rate the usefulness of intermediate actions taken during generation—like which papers to retrieve, which sections to add, or how to explain ideas—obscuring the actions users prefer. Thus, we lack datasets to analyze and learn which intermediate actions are useful for DR.

We release DRACULA:22 2 To spare readers our backronym: Deep Research Action Corpus via User-in-the-Loop Annotation the first open-source dataset with user feedback for understanding the actions users want DR systems to take. Over five weeks and 450 annotation hours, 19 researchers ask queries to a DR system (Singh et al., 2025b) that proposes actions—decisions the agent can take to improve how reports answer user queries (e.g., “Explain concepts with analogies”, “Add a section on datasets”). For each query, users pick the actions they want for their report, then view a report tailored to their selections to judge whether actions were executed effectively (Figure 1). In total, DRACULA has 8,103 binary selections as preferences on proposed actions and 5,230 binary judgments for action execution, each with rationales (section 2).

We first ensure DR systems can realistically execute the actions in DRACULA. Users rate our tested models as more successful at executing selected actions than at proposing useful ones (section 3.1), and qualitative analyses reveal system limitations are a rare reason for rejecting actions (section 3.2). Thus, a key challenge in DR is not just executing actions, but knowing which actions users want executed—motivating the rest of our paper’s focus on studying the latter.

To further analyze user action selections, we measure their predictability via simulation experiments (Seshadri et al., 2026): given an action, can LLMs predict whether users select it, and what improves these predictions? Practically, reliable predictions can serve as training rewards (Shao et al., 2025) and benchmark metrics (Liang et al., 2025) to improve DR actions.

Baseline few-shot prompting with five frontier LLM judges initially struggles to predict the actions users select (section 4.2). Deeper experiments show predictions improve most when using the user’s entire past selection history rather than extrapolated, self-reported, and cold-start user contexts like research papers and stated preferences—indicating simulations benefit most from user context closer to the task format (section 4.3). To determine whether our models have reached simulation’s upper bound, we run a follow-up study and show users disagree with their past selections as their goals change (section 4.4). Thus, certain users’ preferences are inherently unpredictable and may always need affordances to clarify them in DR systems.

Finally, motivated by the benefits of user-specific context in action prediction, we evaluate whether three sources of user context—past research papers, stated preferences, and revealed preferences from past selections—can improve action generation. Users most often select actions generated from their revealed preferences (section 5), highlighting the value of learning from past interactions to improve DR actions, and more generally, the potential for offline simulation experiments to inform online interventions that can make agents more useful.

Overall, while researchers extensively study how well DR systems can execute actions, we show a key bottleneck is predicting which actions users want in the first place—a difficult task that largely benefits from user-specific modeling. More broadly, as execution horizons scale, agents must take increasingly complex actions to support users, making intermediate feedback beyond the final output key for improving their utility. Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    DRACULA, the first large-scale dataset of user feedback on intermediate DR actions, including queries, actions, user selections, execution judgments, and user contexts.

  2. 2.

    A new simulation task for LLMs to predict the actions users want DR systems to take.

  3. 3.

    Evidence that selected actions are highly-user specific and change based on user goals, and that simulation experiments can guide online interventions to make DR more useful.

2 DRACULA: Inviting Users for Feedback on Deep Research Actions

To improve DR, we rely on user feedback that can teach systems how to generate reports users prefer (Ouyang et al., 2022). Most DR feedback only scores the report (Zhao et al., 2025a), but producing reports requires many intermediate actions, like which papers to retrieve, which sections to include, and how to explain ideas (Pan et al., 2026). Report-level feedback alone provides little insight on which of these actions users prefer (Movva et al., 2026), making it difficult to study and learn which actions DR should take to support users.

To address this, we explicitly gather feedback on natural language actions that describe how DR agents could improve reports (e.g., “Find new datasets”, “Add deployment tips”). In our feedback protocol, users issue a query and we propose actions for them to select from. We then show a report reflecting the selected actions, which users judge for execution quality (Figure 1). We host our annotation in a DR interface to build DRACULA: a dataset of DR queries, actions, and feedback split into action selections and executions, described next.

Query Selection: To reflect real DR usage without manually writing queries, annotators select 50 queries of interest from a set asked by users in the deployed ScholarQA system (Singh et al., 2025b). We label all queries by field/subfield with Gemini-2.5 Flash (e.g., “AI”/“AI Agents”) to help annotators search. For each query qq, annotators self-report their intent for selecting qq—paper search, learning, brainstorming, implementation design, or writing—and expertise from 1–5.

Action Generation: For each qq, we randomly prompt one of GPT-4.1, Claude-4 Sonnet, Gemini-2.5 Flash, or DeepSeek-V3 to create eight actions 𝒜={a1,…,a8}\mathcal{A}=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{8}\} (Prompt A.7). We use actions as they clearly describe how a DR system will attempt to improve a report, unlike other designs such as follow-up questions that focus on clarifying intent (Wang et al., 2025a).

Prior work shows user context improves clarifications (Feng et al., 2023; Montazeralghaem et al., 2025), so we test whether this benefits action generation. We use research papers as user context, commonly studied in scientific tasks similar to DR (Kreutz & Schenkel, 2022; Mysore et al., 2023). For each qq, we create four generic actions that condition on qq, and four paper actions that also condition on annotator-picked papers 𝒫\mathcal{P} reflecting their interests. Varied prompt contexts also boosts output diversity (Kim et al., 2023), desirable in feedback data (Lambert et al., 2024). We de-duplicate actions across conditions with GPT-4.1 (Prompt A.7).

Our actions span four qualitative categories (the center of Figure 1 has examples) with common instruction types that users add to queries to improve DR reports (Haddad et al., 2026): Content (what the report covers), Style (how the report is written), Specificity (how to treat the query scope), and Research Ideas (how to adapt to the researcher’s goals). To ensure coverage, we generate one generic and one paper action per category (i.e., four each, eight in total).

Annotators view 𝒜\mathcal{A} as a checklist (Figure 6) grouped by category and mark which actions 𝒜′⊆𝒜\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{A} they want the agent to take and a rationale, yielding lselect∈{0,1}l_{\text{select}}\in\{0,1\} (Figure 1, left).

Report Generation: We use the MyScholarQA system from Balepur et al. (2026), backed by Claude-4 Sonnet.33 3 The system is open-sourced with a demo: https://personalized-scholarqa.apps.allenai.org/. It creates a report to answer qq by retrieving Semantic Scholar papers, re-ranking, extracting evidence, planning outlines, and generating sections. MyScholarQA alters ScholarQA to use 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime} as input at each step (Appendix A.1). To aid annotation, we highlight spans in the report where each action is applied (Figure 7). Annotators judge whether each a∈𝒜′a\in\mathcal{A}^{\prime} was executed well and a rationale, giving lexec∈{0,1}l_{\text{exec}}\in\{0,1\} (Figure 1, right).

User Study: We recruit 20 CS researchers in diverse fields (e.g., Security, CV, NLP, CompBio, AI Ethics) from Upwork, verified as active DR users via a pilot survey. We run a five week study over ~450 hours at $30–45/hour, approved by our IRB. As quality control, we omit ten queries that are not in scope for DR (e.g., “How to DR”), and one annotator who reused rationales, yielding 8,103 selections for lselectl_{\text{select}} and 5,230 judgments for lexecl_{\text{exec}}.44 4 In total, DRACULA contains 902 unique queries and 7731 unique actions.

3 Generating Actions is a High-Stakes Challenge for Deep Research

We first verify that DR systems can execute the actions in DRACULA, ensuring execution quality does not largely impact our future analyses of user preferences on actions. We first compare how well models generate versus execute actions, showing that they struggle more on the former (section 3.1). Qualitative analyses further reveal that system limitations are a rare reason for rejecting actions (section 3.2), motivating our later studies on user-preferred actions (section 4).

3.1 Neglecting Action Generation Can Drain the Usefulness of Deep Research

The proportion of actions that users rate as well-executed in reports exceeds the proportion of actions they pick (Figure 2): LLMs struggle to infer actions users want, but more reliably execute actions once specified. Extensive work aims to improve DR executions (Wei et al., 2025), but another key challenge lies in learning what to execute—a gap DRACULA fills.

We also note despite prior work showing the benefits of using papers as user context (Mysore et al., 2023), paper actions are selected less than generic. section 5 tests this further by studying more user contexts.

As initial analyses, we group action selection rates by user intent, action type, and generator LLM. Actions altering report content and style are generally preferred over specificity or research ideas; Claude and DeepSeek generate the latter less effectively (Figure 3, right). Writing intent queries have lower selection rates, but intuitively, users prefer style actions more often (Figure 3, left). Notably, Claude-4 Sonnet backs report generation in MyScholarQA but this LLM still has low action selection rates, so action generation being less successful than execution holds when controlling for LLM.

3.2 Qualitative Analysis: An Initial Taste of Action Generation

To study and better illustrate the data in DRACULA, we run qualitative analyses under two research questions: RQ1—Which actions do users select? and RQ2—Why are actions not selected?

RQ1—What actions do users select? We run a semi-automated qualitative coding procedure (Bingham, 2023; Lam et al., 2024). Claude-4.6 Opus infers clusters with high-level action types from 200 random actions per user, then merges duplicate clusters. Two authors refine clusters, then Gemini-3 Flash assigns each action to the most relevant cluster (Appendix A.6).

The most often selected actions summarize key points and compare papers (Table 1, top), aiding comprehension (Erera et al., 2019), while the least selected propose practical tools and cross-domain connections (Table 1, bottom). From users’ rationales, tools were often rejected due to intent misalignment (e.g., “No code snippets are required, as this is a theoretical question”). Cross-domain connections were rejected when models over-personalize to user papers, degrading clarity (e.g., “This is related to my research but I don’t think what the model is suggesting is even a thing”). In only 19 cases, users cited DR system limitations as the reason for rejecting an action and never showed “miswanting” (Gilbert & Wilson, 2000)—realizing they did not want an action—suggesting most rejections reflect true action dispreferences.

RQ2: Why are actions not selected? Applying the same coding procedure on rationales for unselected actions, we surface 15 failure modes. The most common involve miscalibrating query scope (Table 2): actions are rejected when they aggressively narrow search, expand beyond the user’s needs, drift off-topic, or neglect user goals. Thus, action generation relies on user-specific context, which we keep in mind when designing future analyses (section 4, section 5).

4 Mirroring User Feedback on Action Selection

We analyze user preferences on DRACULA’s actions via user simulations: given an action, can LLMs predict whether users will select it? Such analyses reveal how predictable user preferences are, and what drives this predictability. Practically, user simulations are more scalable than real user feedback (Wu et al., 2025), so reliable predictions could form training rewards (Shao et al., 2025) and benchmark metrics (Liang et al., 2025) to improve DR actions.

We turn DRACULA into reusable evaluations that test whether LLMs can predict the actions users select (section 4.1). We first run prompt baselines, showing predicting action selection initially struggles (section 4.2). We then test varied modeling choices to improve predictions and reveal they improve most when using a user’s past selections (section 4.3). We finally see whether models have reached the inherent predictability in DRACULA by studying user consistency (section 4.4).

4.1 Turning DRACULA into a User Simulation Task

We define a classification task called action prediction for simulating user selections: Given a query qq and proposed action aa, predict l^select∈{0,1}\hat{l}_{\text{select}}\in\{0,1\}, indicating whether the user selected aa.

We sort our data chronologically (oldest to newest) and use 80/10/10 splits based on qq, giving 5982/1140/918 examples for train/dev/test with a 0.32/0.68 test split for 0/1 labels. We omit noisy test set items where GPT-5 cannot predict the true label via the user’s rationale or where we flag low-quality queries (section 2); this impacts <5% of the data. We report Macro-F1 score—the unweighted average of per-class F1—commonly used for binary judges in DR (Sharma et al., 2025), and standard error via bootstrap sampling with n=500n=500 (Efron, 1992).

4.2 Evaluating Action Prediction Off the Bat

We assess five strong baseline LLM judges on action prediction: GPT-5, Claude-4.6 Opus, Gemini-3.0 Pro, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen-3 235B Thinking (Appendix A.1). The prompt describes the task and requests a JSON with a 0/1 prediction and explanation (Prompts A.7), and uses 1000 few-shot (q,a,lselect)(q,a,l_{\text{select}}) training examples randomly sampled across all users.

F1 scores do not largely exceed a random 50/50 baseline across LLMs (Figure 4), especially on generic actions, showing judges have room to improve in action prediction; we explore this next (section 4.3). Action prediction on paper actions has higher F1, so LLMs may more reliably distinguish differences in preferred versus dispreferred actions that tailor to user context.

4.3 Awakening Action Prediction Capabilities

To improve action prediction (section 4.2), we now assess different modeling choices. Motivated by user-specific action generation flaws in section 3.2, we test adding user context, along with general analyses on trivial baselines, retrieval, and task engineering. To limit costs, we use GPT-5 only, a strong LLM in Figure 4, but Appendix A.3 runs a subset of analyses with more LLMs.

Action Prediction is Non-Trivial. We verify the task is unsolvable via simple cues. Trivial baselines—GPT-5 prompted without the query and action as partial-input baselines (Poliak et al., 2018), and an SVM trained with TF-IDF embeddings (Sparck Jones, 1972)—score near random (Table 3, Trivial Baselines), so action prediction needs more than shallow reasoning.

User History is Key. As action selection varies by user (section 3.1), we test whether conditioning on past selections from just the target user aids predictions. This largely boosts F1 (Table 3, User-Specific History vs All User History), so user modeling benefits the task. Fewer examples and simple user selection priors do not explain these gains: the same number of examples over all user selections or just giving selection rates (e.g., “this user picks 71% of actions”) lower F1 (Table 3, Context Engineering), so having the text of actions is useful  (Shaikh et al., 2026). We thus adopt user-specific history as the baseline for the remaining experiments.

Other User Context Types Don’t Cut It. We evaluate whether more user context improves action prediction. Augmenting user-specific history prompts with user-selected papers in section 2, action labels (e.g., “Content”, “Style”), past rationales, and reported intent/expertise never largely beat the user history baseline (Table 3, Feature Engineering), except for a small but insignificant boost from rationales. Thus, user behavior that is closer to the task is a stronger predictive signal for future behavior versus self-reported user descriptors (Binz et al., 2024).

Actions Speak Louder than Words. LLMs may struggle to infer the latent preferences from user’s action history that drive their future selections (Samuelson, 1938), degrading action predictions. To test this, we first elicit our users’ stated preferences (Hensher, 1994)—five high-level rules our users write to describe their ideal DR system after having interacted with our system (e.g., “Introductions must follow academic paper structures”). We then use these as input for action prediction and compare this to giving five rules GPT infers from each user’s past selections. GPT rules are more predictive than user-written rules, but neither exceeds user-specific history (Table 3, Stated Preferences). Thus, capturing how users actually select actions is more predictive than the actions they say they prefer (Chung et al., 2025).

Long Context is Unlikely to be the Main Culprit. Action prediction models reason over lengthy user selections, raising concerns on long-context limitations (Laban et al., 2026). We test this by shortening input context via: 1) randomly sampling 50 examples; or 2) retrieving the top-50 relevant examples via GritLM (Muennighoff et al., 2025) and a GPT-5 reranker (Sun et al., 2023). Neither method improves F1 (Table 3, Long-Context Management), but F1 is not much worse, so selection histories could be compressed while maintaining predictive power for efficiency (Sun et al., 2025). Appendix A.4 shows similar trends for k∈{10,100}k\in\{10,100\}.

Framing the Task as Ranking Does Not Help Much. Binary judgments are hard in isolation because they use implicit cutoffs; relative comparisons are often easier (Liu, 2009). We thus test alternative formulations of action prediction: (1) jointly labeling all actions per query, mirroring our annotation; and (2) pairwise comparisons over all action pairs—ranking by ELO score with a validation-tuned cutoff. Neither format significantly beats the user-history baseline (Table 3, Task Engineering), so action prediction’s difficulty is not just its task format.

Takeaway: Action prediction is tough but tractable, largely improving with user-specific history. Conversely, extra user features, long-context management, and varied task formats offer limited gains beyond this. For researchers building user simulators, Table 3 shows behavior from the user mirroring the task is the most predictive signal versus self-reported and extrapolated user context, despite their common use in simulations (Wang et al., 2025b).

4.4 The Limits of Action Prediction: User Preferences are Far from Immortal

Given our improved action prediction scores in section 4.3, we now test whether our LLMs are at the limit of what is inherently predictable in DRACULA by measuring our users’ preference stability. To test this, 18 annotators re-label four of their queries in the first study, re-selecting the actions they prefer. We run this five months after the first study to limit memory effects.

User stability—predicting initial user selections from their new ones—has F1=0.672, near GPT-5 on the same subset using user-specific history (0.664), but errors differ in action types and users. User stability F1 is closer between generic and paper actions (0.681 and 0.664, respectively) than GPT (0.638 and 0.689). Per-user, stability ranges from as low as 0.434 (user 5) to as high as 0.823 (user 3) and 0.945 (user 8) F1. While GPT-5 improves F1 over less stable users, it struggles in action prediction on stable ones (Figure 5)—so there is still headroom for F1 on stable users.

Changes in user selections are not just noise. Analyzing rationales, one user initially selected the action “Interpret hallucinations as generative distribution mismatch problems”, but later decided not to, as they were now “interested in solutions, not new insights”—indicating a shift in intent. Similarly, one user initially picked the action “Start with concise definitions of fall detection” as it was “perfect for their audience”, but later did not since they “already know what a fall is”; their preference changed based on whether they were reading the report (i.e., versus sharing it).

Action prediction is inherently bounded by latent shifts in users’ intent and audience (Fan et al., 2020). For such users, clarification mechanisms such as our actions remain practical, enabling them to customize report generation in ways models cannot reliably anticipate.

5 Richer User Contexts Can Feed Personalized Action Generation

We now use our offline results to improve action generation, “closing the loop” (Belz et al., 2021) by better aligning actions with user preferences. Our analyses recurringly motivate personalization (Brusilovsky, 1996)—action generation flaws often stem from user-specific intent (section 3.2) and selection history improves simulation (section 4.3)—suggesting action generation can benefit from user-specific context. However, our first cold-start personalization attempt via papers was subpar (section 3.1), so we also test two user contexts that more closely mirror DR interactions: (1) stated preferences from section 4.3; and (2) revealed preferences (Samuelson, 1938)—queries, actions, and judgments users previously provided as few-shot examples.

Eighteen annotators write ten more queries to ask our DR system. For each query, we generate four actions conditioned on each of our four user contexts (generic, paper, stated preferences, revealed preferences) with GPT-4.1—a strong model in Figure 3—yielding 16 in total. Given the variance of selection rates over qualitative action types (section 3.1), we no longer enforce type diversity. GPT-4.1 de-duplicates the actions across contexts. Annotators then pick actions they would want the DR system to execute with rationales, just like section 2.

Selection rates for actions from stated and revealed preferences exceed paper actions (Table 4). Research papers are not tied to DR interactions, highlighting the challenge of finding useful cold-start personalization signals for DR (Zhao et al., 2025b). The gains from revealed preferences over generic are modest, so generic actions already capture broadly useful behavior. But crucially, personalized action selection rates do not need to exceed generic actions to be useful; personalization yields varied actions—only 12.1% overlap between generic and revealed preferences—that users still pick above random (>50%), expanding the actions DR can take to help users.

We investigate the benefits of revealed preferences via GPT-4.1’s rationales for generated actions, which cite relevant items from the user’s past selections. 80.0% of rationales cite both generic and paper actions in the user’s history, suggesting GPT combines the strengths of varied action types. One action, “Compare CLIP vs other benchmarked VLMs”, merged the user’s preference for comparisons via generic actions (e.g., “Present table showing models”) and the user’s interest in benchmarks found in paper actions (e.g., “Highlight benchmark evaluation”).

Overall, the benefits of past selections show the potential for DR to learn from accumulated interaction data (Li et al., 2010). More broadly, it is promising that gains from user-specific context in action prediction correspond to improvements in generated actions. We encourage future work to explore the extent to which simulation accuracy on real user feedback (Zhou et al., 2026; Seshadri et al., 2026) can inform online interventions to improve agent utility.

6 Digging Up Related Work

Given our paper’s focus on collecting intermediate feedback through generated actions in DR, we bridge prior work in DR evaluation (section 6.1) and intermediate user feedback (section 6.2).

6.1 Evaluating Deep Research Systems

Scientific Deep Research (DR) agents synthesize long-form reports via documents to aid scientific research (Team et al., 2025). By combining retrievers and LLMs (Asai et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Lála et al., 2023), such agents can create varied report formats like Wikipedia articles (Liu et al., 2018), expository texts (Jiang et al., 2025), and surveys (Yan et al., 2025).

Beyond excelling on benchmarks (Wei et al., 2025; Chandrahasan et al., 2025), training and evaluating with user feedback is a gold standard for improving DR (Ouyang et al., 2022; Touvron et al., 2023). Most protocols rely on ratings (Li et al., 2025b; Hwang et al., 2026) or preferences (Zhao et al., 2025a; Miroyan et al., 2025; Du et al., 2026) to collect user feedback on reports, but this feedback does not directly target the intermediate actions DR agents take (Zhong et al., 2026)—retrieving papers, planning sections, and writing reports—obscuring the actions users prefer. While some works reconstruct intermediate feedback based on user judgments over the final response (Garbacea & Tan, 2025; Joshi et al., 2025; Findeis et al., 2025), these are hypotheses and not confirmed by users (Li et al., 2025a). DRACULA instead directly collects feedback on actions user prefer for DR, along with their execution quality.

6.2 Intermediate User Feedback

Researchers have long recognized the weaknesses of user feedback on final outputs (Hosking et al., 2024), and have thus designed protocols to collect more informative signals. Examples include fine-grained and multi-dimensional feedback (Wu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a), improved specification in annotation protocols (Dipper et al., 2004; Malaviya et al., 2025), and richer signals from downstream interactions (Mozannar et al., 2025; Shaikh et al., 2026).

In DR, intermediate feedback is rarely collected. Works design multi-aspect rubrics for DR queries (Lv et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026b; Sharma et al., 2025; Gunjal et al., 2025), but they are often designed by experts to score objectively high-quality behaviors, not subjective user preferences. Balepur et al. (2026) and Pan et al. (2026) also generate actions for DR but evaluate them only via qualitative interviews, in contrast to our large-scale feedback collection and simulation experiments. Chandrahasan et al. (2025) release a DR feedback platform and 1,281 votes on tool calls in agent execution traces (e.g., “Scraped five web pages…”), but this setup mainly evaluates execution quality. Conversely, DRACULA is the first dataset with 8,310 points of feedback for understanding which actions users want DR systems to execute.

Outside of DR, the closest line of work is process reward modeling (Lightman et al., 2024, PRMs), which gathers step-level feedback on model reasoning (Zhang et al., 2025) or agent traces (Zhang et al., 2026) to reward strong executions. DRACULA’s action feedback is similar in spirit, but unlike PRMs’ focus on improving how a chosen trajectory is executed, our feedback guides which trajectories an agent should follow. This makes action feedback closer to query reformulation (Li et al., 2024): actions are evaluated before being executed, while feedback in PRMs typically scales with the number of steps in the execution trace.

7 Conclusion: Ignoring the Actions Users Want is a Grave Mistake

We release DRACULA: a dataset of user feedback on intermediate actions in DR, moving beyond the default protocol of only evaluating DR reports. Our data shows systems cannot fully anticipate the actions users select for DR, but can execute them well once specified.

Generating useful actions is underexplored, but DRACULA enables models for predicting ones users want DR to take. When reliable, such methods can form rewards in new training methods or benchmarks (Shao et al., 2025). Toward this, we reveal the dominance of user-specific history for action prediction, motivating new research in user context: managing long action selection history (Wang et al., 2024c), discovering better signals than papers in cold-start settings (Zhao et al., 2025b), and inferring preferences as text (Ryan et al., 2025).

Our success in action execution does not imply it is solved. Challenges remains in improving execution as user requests grow complex (Pham et al., 2024). The actions users do not pick can reveal execution gaps for future work. While rare in DRACULA, users avoided some actions (e.g., “Add code snippets”) they knew the DR system could not execute (section 3.2), showing how action-level user feedback can surface emerging execution needs (Haddad et al., 2026).

More broadly, our decomposition offers a scalable way to collect feedback in complex agents: articulating potential actions users can endorse, then executing them in the final output. Since action generation only requires specifying the types of actions that the end agent can execute, feedback on actions can be collected independently to execution improvements. As agent horizons grow (METR, 2026), action-level feedback will become increasingly crucial for making agents more helpful to users. DRACULA represents one step toward this goal.

Ethics Statement

While learning from human feedback can improve user satisfaction in DR, we acknowledge potential risks—especially when considering personalization and user-specific context. Optimizing for actions that users select may instill confirmation bias with what they are already familiar with (Klayman, 1995), raise privacy and stereotyping concerns (Kantharuban et al., 2025), and may lead to responses that are users think are helpful without truly improving downstream outcomes (Mozannar et al., 2025). To help mitigate these risks, we only consider user outputs contexts tied to our system (e.g., research papers, stated preferences) and not sensitive information, and our organization’s IRB approved the entire user study design.

We also acknowledge that our results only directly apply to our specific setting of Deep Research with CS researchers. As the first study on action-level feedback in DR and given the cost of our user studies, we primarily study CS, following prior work (Bragg et al., 2025). Future work should ensure our results generalize to their desired personalization tasks and user populations before deploying any of the interventions we study in this work.

We use Generative AI in this project. We use Cursor to help implement experiments and modify the style of plots, and ChatGPT to help refine paper writing.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Model Configurations

For action generation in data collection and user studies (section 2, section 3), we use the following model endpoints in LiteLLM:

  • •

    GPT-4.1 (Achiam et al., 2023): openai/gpt-4.1-2025-04-14

  • •

    Gemini-2.5 Flash (Comanici et al., 2025): gemini/gemini-2.5-flash

  • •

    Claude-4 Sonnet (Anthropic, 2025): anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514

  • •

    Deepseek-V3 (Liu et al., 2024): together_ai/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3

We generate with default parameters. To incentivize diversity during data collection, we generate twice as many actions (e.g., eight generic actions, eight paper-based actions), then randomly sample four of each action type, similar to overgenerate-and-rerank pipelines (Hu et al., 2024). We detect duplicate actions between the generic and paper-based action types with GPT-4.1 (Prompt A.7), giving credit to both action types if selected, and resampling another random action to ensure the total number of actions reaches eight. When experimenting with different user contexts in section 5, we only generate four actions of each type and run the same de-duplication process.

For action prediction and action execution experiments (section 4), we use the following model endpoints in LiteLLM:

  • •

    Claude-4.6 Opus (Anthropic, 2026): anthropic/claude-opus-4-6

  • •

    Gemini-3 Pro (Google, 2025): gemini/gemini-3-pro-preview

  • •

    GPT-5 (Singh et al., 2025a): openai/gpt-5-2025-08-07

  • •

    DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025): together_ai/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1

  • •

    Qwen-3 235B Thinking (Yang et al., 2025): together_ai/Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507

We generate with a temperature of 1.01.0, reasoning effort set to “medium” (or equivalents), and a maximum token length of 81920 (but override this for models with lower maximum token lengths).

For Deep Research report generation, we adapt the open-source ScholarQA pipeline from Ai2 (Singh et al., 2025b). The system exposes functions for rewriting queries, planning an outline of section titles, and generating sections iteratively. We minimally modify prompts in these functions so that they also have access to all of the user’s selected actions, instead of just the query. Our preliminary testing found that this led to slightly higher instruction-following versus concatenating all actions with the input query. However, the later still was effective, so it is feasible for future work to run action feedback collection similar to ours but treating the end agent as a fully black box without modifying any parts of the agent trace.

A.2 User Interface

We provide screenshots of the interface annotators use for evaluating action generation (Figure 6 and action execution (Figure 7). The interface was built by extending the companion web app to the ScholarQA system (Singh et al., 2025b). The interface was built by extending the companion web app to the ScholarQA system (Singh et al., 2025b).

A.3 Further Comparisons of Action and Execution Prediction

Along with action prediction, we also experiment with execution prediction—where LLMs must predict whether a user judged an action as being executed well (0/1) given the report, query, and action. We provide further results on action prediction and execution prediction across more LLMs, metrics, zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies, and action types in Table 5 and Table 6, respectively. Our results support section 4.2 across these settings: action prediction largely improves when models access user-specific history, but the task still has lower scores than execution prediction.

A.4 Further Evaluations of Action Prediction with Retrieval

We further explore the benefits of retrieval for long-context management in action prediction. We replicate our experiments in section 4.3 with k∈{10,100}k\in\{10,100\} and introduce two new retrieval baselines: retrieving the kk-oldest examples from the user’s history and the kk-newest examples. Overall, our findings are consistent (Table 7): retrieval minimally improves F1 scores in some cases, but the fact that retrieval even with k=10k=10 does not largely degrade scores shows there is room to improve efficiency for user modeling in the task.

A.5 Further Evaluations of Action Prediction with Stated Preferences

We explore how well other LLMs can infer rules from a user’s action history and apply them for predictions, following the procedure of Stated Preferences in section 4.3. Overall, trends are consistent: user-specific history dominates in F1, and model-inferred rules are more useful for predictions than user-stated rules.

A.6 Clustering Procedure

We now detail the qualitative clustering procedure used in section 3.2. Our process is inspired by qualitative coding (Bingham, 2023). We first prompt Claude-4.6 Sonnet to use 200 random examples from each user’s history to derive high-level clusters describing either actions (Prompt A.7) or rationales (Prompt A.7). We then prompt the model to merge all per-user clusters into higher-level themes, forming a global taxonomy (Prompt A.7). The first and last author reviewed all clusters and discarded low-quality ones (e.g., “Add Specific Content Section” for action clusters, as it overlaps with categories like “Restructure Organization”).

Finally, we have Gemini-3-Flash take each individual action and rationale and classify which cluster it belongs to (Prompt A.7 with temperature equal to 0.00.0. One author reviewed 50 random classification outputs across 500 examples for action and rationale labeling. They agreed with the classifier in 98% of cases for action clustering and 90% of cases for rationale clustering.

A.7 Prompts

To encourage reproducibility during the review process, we provide the prompts used in our experiments here, but encourage readers to access our Github upon release to access them more easily.

For action generation, we provide prompts for generic action generation (Prompt A.7), paper-based action generation (Prompt A.7), rule-based action generation (Prompt A.7), history-based action generation (Prompt A.7). During data collection, the generic and paper-based prompts must generate a fixed number of actions and evenly distributed to the following qualitative action types:

  • •

    Content: Specifies what information the response should include and how it should be conceptually framed.

  • •

    Explanation Style: Specifies the style of the response and how the explanation for the information is communicated.

  • •

    Specificity: Clarifies and narrows the scope of the response to better match the researcher’s intended focus.

  • •

    Usefulness (Research Ideas): Shapes the response to be actionable or instrumental for the researcher’s goals or workflow.

and the following implementation types, which are given to different steps in SQA so it knows how to alter reports:

  • •

    Search Add: Personalizes the search by adding new terms or dimensions to the original query.

  • •

    Search Refine: Personalizes the search by revising or improving the original query.

  • •

    Organization: Personalizes how the papers are grouped into sections for the final response.

  • •

    Generation: Personalizes how certain sections are written and explained.

During the user study in section 5, we do not fix the distribution of the qualitative action types. We also provide our prompts for de-duplication (Prompt A.7).

For clustering, we provide our generation prompts for action clusters (Prompt A.7) and rationale clusters (Prompt A.7), merging clusters per user (Prompt A.7), and labeling new actions and rationales according to existing cluster labels (Prompt A.7).

Finally, we provide action prediction prompts in binary classification (Prompt A.7), ranking (Prompt A.7), and pairwise comparison (Prompt A.7) task formats. We also provide our action execution prompt (Prompt A.7) and prompt for inferring rules from the user’s action selection history (Prompt A.7). We tailor these prompts for all of the experiments in section 4.3, such as when we add new features.
